note.explanation: Plants adjust how water moves into or out of their cells to survive in different habitats. Hydrophytes remove excess water, xerophytes reduce water loss, and halophytes take up salts to prevent water leaving their cells.
note.checkAnswer: Hydrophytes remove extra water through stomata on floating leaves; halophytes absorb salts to make their bodies hypertonic and prevent water loss.
note.simple: Plants have different ways to manage water depending on where they live. Wet-habitat plants get rid of extra water, desert plants conserve water, and salt-habitat plants adjust their salt levels.
note.checkQuestion: How do halophytes stop water from moving out of their cells?
note.title: Osmotic Adjustments in Plants
steps: Recall the water problem in that habitat.
Describe the adjustment the plant makes.
note.answer: Halophytes absorb salts from outside and make their bodies hypertonic, so water does not move out of their cells.

modelAnswer: Hydrophytes live in freshwater or in wet soil, and absorption of water occurs through the whole surface.
Many hydrophytes have broad floating leaves with many stomata on their upper surfaces; water moves out through these stomata.
Xerophytes live in extremely dry environments and have deep roots to absorb water from almost dry soil.
Their body surface has very few stomata and is covered with a thick waxy cuticle to reduce water loss.
Some xerophytes store water in specialized stems or roots called succulent organs.
Halophytes live in salty habitats and absorb salts from outside to make their bodies hypertonic.
In this way, water does not move out of their cells; excess salt can be stored in cells or excreted from salt glands on leaves.

steps.text: Such plants absorb salts from outside and make their bodies hypertonic.

explain.title: Mesophytes
explain.body: Mesophytes are the terrestrial plants which are adapted to survive in moderate environment that are neither too dry nor too wet. They have well-developed roots that absorb water efficiently, a cuticle that minimizes water loss, and stomata that can close to reduce transpiration. Maize, clover, and rose are examples.

explain.title: Hydrophytes
explain.body: Hydrophytes live in freshwater (ponds, and lakes etc.) or in wet soil. In these plants, the absorption of water occurs through the whole surface. Many have broad floating leaves with many stomata on their upper surfaces, through which water moves out. Water lily is a common example.

explain.title: Xerophytes
explain.body: Xerophytes live in extremely dry environments (deserts). They have deep roots to absorb water from almost dry soil, very few stomata, and a thick waxy cuticle to reduce water loss. Some store water in soft, juicy specialized stems or roots called succulent organs.

explain.title: Halophytes
explain.body: Halophytes live in habitats with salty waters, such as the sea or salty marshes. They absorb salts from outside and make their bodies hypertonic, so water does not move out of their cells. Excess salt can be stored in cells or excreted from salt glands on leaves.

mistakes: Do not mix up the habitats: hydrophytes live in freshwater or wet soil, while halophytes live in salty water habitats.
Do not say that xerophytes have many stomata; they have very few stomata and a thick waxy cuticle.
Do not confuse a succulent organ with a salt gland: succulent stems or roots store water, while salt glands excrete salt.
For halophytes, include that they absorb salts and become hypertonic; simply saying that they live in salty water is incomplete.
When describing hydrophytes, state that water moves out through stomata on the upper surfaces of floating leaves.
